clips.text_zh: 成日都係咁，睇住BTC唔郁幾星期，理都唔理，點知一pump 15%就個個衝入去。點解永遠都係升完先買？其實我都係嗰啲人…prop firm又燒多咗一注。又是學費🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Why buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks, ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened?
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread asking why people FOMO into BTC after the move

signal.rationale: Post-hoc observation on retail FOMO, no actionable setup

clips.text_en_b2: It happens every single cycle, and frankly I'm sick of falling for it. You watch BTC flatline for weeks on end, completely dismiss it as dead money, and the moment it pumps 15% out of nowhere, suddenly everyone's rushing in. Why is it that retail always ends up buying after the move? I got liquidated on my prop firm account chasing the breakout — another expensive lesson in chasing green candles.
clips.text_en_c1: The irony of retail behaviour never ceases to astound me. Bitcoin sits dormant for weeks on end, and not a soul gives it a second glance; the moment it rallies fifteen percent, however, every self-proclaimed contrarian scrambles to pile in. The pattern is almost comical in its predictability, which makes it all the more infuriating when one catches oneself doing exactly the same thing yet again. The prop firm evaluation account bled another deposit this morning, and the lesson, as always, comes billed as tuition. Were timing markets genuinely possible, one suspects the cycle would be considerably less painful; alas, it is not, and the fee keeps climbing.
clips.text_en_c2: There is a rather exasperating rhythm to retail crypto behaviour, one so predictable that even seasoned participants cannot feign surprise. Bitcoin idles for weeks on end, languishing in narrow ranges while the broader cohort pays it no mind whatsoever; then, almost as though cued by an invisible conductor, it surges fifteen per cent in a single move, and the selfsame cohort scrambles to pile in at precisely the wrong juncture. The irony is hardly lost on anyone, least of all those of us who have, once again, contributed to the pattern. Another allocation has evaporated in the prop firm account, another tuition fee rendered to the market, and one cannot help but wonder whether reflexivity itself is the only strategy consistently guaranteed to lose money.

clips.text_zh: 睇到呢個數字真係想喊。15年前放1k USD入Bitcoin，今日值897萬美金。我而家30歲，望住prop firm賬戶每日流血😭😭😭。早知讀書嗰陣all in啦…起碼我仲係STEM guy不是嗎lol
clips.text_en_b1: $1,000 invested 15 years ago today would be worth: Bitcoin $8,970,000, Nvidia $735,000, Tesla $231,000, Apple $29,000, S&P $8,400, Gold $2,150. Posted on /biz/ this week as a reality check on missed gains.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ comparison of 15-year returns across major assets

signal.rationale: Implied BTC bias from the returns comparison, long-term hold thesis

clips.text_en_b2: Stumbling across these numbers genuinely hit me hard. A thousand bucks parked in Bitcoin fifteen years ago would be sitting at roughly 8.97 million today, whereas Nvidia would have turned it into 735k and Tesla around 231k. Even gold barely cracked 2k from that same grand, and the S&P scraped together just 8,400. I'm thirty now, bleeding out in a prop firm account daily, and honestly wishing I'd gone all-in instead of chasing STEM degrees.
clips.text_en_c1: Staring at that historical returns table genuinely brought a lump to my throat. A single thousand dollars allocated to Bitcoin fifteen years ago would, at present valuations, sit comfortably at roughly 8.97 million; Nvidia holdings would have appreciated to around 735,000, Tesla to 231,000, and even Apple to a respectable 29,000, whereas the S&P would have yielded a measly 8,400 and gold barely 2,150. Now thirty, I watch my prop firm account haemorrhage capital on a daily basis while consoling myself with the thought that, had I had the conviction back then, the trajectory might have differed. A STEM background does offer some solace, though admittedly not financial compensation.
clips.text_en_c2: The juxtaposition of figures is enough to induce a kind of melancholic vertigo in anyone under the age of forty. A modest one thousand dollars committed fifteen years ago would, were it lodged in Bitcoin, now be worth approximately eight point nine seven million; Nvidia shares would have yielded seven hundred and thirty-five thousand; Tesla, two hundred and thirty-one thousand; Apple a comparatively pedestrian twenty-nine thousand; the S&P a respectable eight thousand four hundred; and gold, the supposed store of value, a rather deflating two thousand one hundred and fifty. Posted to /biz/ as a sobering reality check, the figures underscore, with brutal clarity, the opportunity cost of hesitation.

clips.text_zh: OpenAI出咗GPT-6 Astra，話乜嘢「AGI era」welcome。wtf。我surveying嘅工會唔會被AI取代先？Tommy同Sum Ho都仲用緊Excel…考牌嘅嘢AI會唔會直接做埋😭 靠AI續命啦我
clips.text_en_b1: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, calling it the most intelligent and aligned model yet. Benchmarks show it nearly saturates ARC AGI 3. The company says welcome to the AGI era. Thread on /g/ called it the strongest AI model ever released.
clips.text_en_b2: So OpenAI finally dropped GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, and they're acting like we've officially crossed into the AGI era. The benchmarks are supposedly nearly saturating ARC AGI 3, which sounds impressive on paper, although I'm struggling to see how that helps my surveying workflow get done faster. Tommy and Sum Ho are still grinding away in Excel while I'm wondering whether AI will eventually sit the licensing exams for us. At this point I'm basically clinging to AI tools for survival.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, describing it in characteristically grandiose terms as the most capable and aligned model to date, with internal benchmarks suggesting it nearly saturates the notoriously demanding ARC-AGI 3 evaluation suite. The company has, rather breathlessly, welcomed users to what it insists is the AGI era, a claim that has predictably divided opinion across the relevant threads on /g/. My surveying colleagues Tommy and Sum Ho continue to labour away in Excel, blissfully unaware, and one cannot help but wonder whether the professional examinations themselves might eventually fall within the model's remit.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has unveiled GPT-6 Astra, framing the release as the advent of a new epoch for artificial intelligence, though whether this constitutes genuine arrival or merely another well-orchestrated marketing crescendo remains a matter of considerable debate. Internal benchmarks suggest the model comes tantalisingly close to saturating the ARC-AGI-3 suite, a result the company has leveraged to declare, with characteristic restraint, that the so-called AGI era has begun. Reaction on /g/ ranged from guarded optimism to outright exasperation, with several anons observing that intelligence, however impressive in the abstract, does rather little for those whose professional livelihoods hinge on tasks that remain stubbornly resistant to automation. For surveyors still wedded to Excel and examination candidates memorising by rote, the promised utopia appears, for the moment, distinctly remote.

He said no white man from NZ should ever participate in it, and asked why the British did not shoot all of those savages.
clips.text_en_b2: Some anon over on /pol/ decided to take yet another shot at the New Zealand haka, calling it the cringiest cultural display he's ever come across. He reckons no white man from NZ should ever participate in it, and even dragged the British in for failing to, quote, shoot all of those savages. Honestly it's got nothing to do with me, but as a Hong Konger I've witnessed far more unhinged performances, so haka barely registers.
clips.text_en_c1: The /pol/ boards have predictably produced another gem of cultural commentary, with an anonymous contributor lambasting the New Zealand haka as the most cringeworthy spectacle to have emerged from that corner of the globe. He went on to opine that no white New Zealander should ever participate in the ritual, and rather colourfully questioned why the British had not simply shot all of the so-called savages at the time of colonisation. While the remarks are, of course, utterly unremarkable for that particular forum, those of us familiar with Hong Kong's far more audacious street performances can only smirk; if one has witnessed locals navigating flaming hoops and razor-thin scaffolding, a…
clips.text_en_c2: The cultural skirmishes that surface on /pol/ seldom warrant sustained attention, yet the latest effusion regarding New Zealand's pre-match haka ritual is, in its own unedifying way, rather instructive. One anonymous contributor, evidently aggrieved by the display, proposed that once Chinese influence extends to Wellington, the ceremony ought to be proscribed outright, decrying it as the most cringeworthy spectacle to have emerged from that corner of the globe. He went further, suggesting that no European-descended New Zealander should ever participate, and lamenting that British forces had not, historically, adopted more terminal measures against the practitioners. From the vantage point of Hong Kong, where residents have witnessed far more outlandish public theatrics, the entire controversy registers as faintly quaint, particularly when one ought really to be monitoring US equity futures.

clips.text_zh: lol笑死。以前啲tech bro話未來唔使買console PC，訂閱就得。而家AI直接食晒server資源，又要返去整hardware。當年打LOL S3嗰陣邊諗到呢啲🙃 打機時間都冇…肥仔信叫我打rank我都no time
clips.text_en_b1: Everyone said in the future we would have no dedicated consoles or PCs, and people would just pay for streaming hardware and a subscription. But now the AI tech bros have taken up all the server resources, so they have to keep making dedicated hardware. Its techbros vs streaming bros now, the anon wrote on /v/.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread on AI eating cloud gaming server resources
clips.text_en_b2: The irony is almost too perfect. A few years back every tech bro was preaching that dedicated consoles and gaming PCs would become obsolete, replaced entirely by streaming subscriptions running on rented hardware. Fast forward to today, and AI workloads have basically devoured all the server capacity, forcing manufacturers to keep churning out consumer hardware after all. Back in Season 3 of League I couldn't have pictured this mess, and these days I barely have time to queue up ranked games anyway.
clips.text_en_c1: There is a certain poetic justice in watching the cloud-gaming thesis unravel in real time. A few years ago, every tech evangelist with a podcast and a Patagonia vest insisted that dedicated consoles and gaming rigs would soon become relics, replaced by subscription-based streaming services accessible from any device. Fast forward to the present, and the artificial intelligence boom has hoovered up virtually every available server resource, leaving the streaming evangelists scrambling back to silicon and soldering stations.
clips.text_en_c2: The collapse of cloud gaming's utopian pretensions has been, in retrospect, almost as inevitable as it is darkly amusing. A mere handful of years ago, the prevailing wisdom among Silicon Valley's techno-optimists held that dedicated hardware would become obsolete, that consumers would subscribe to ephemeral streams rather than possess anything tangible, and that the console wars would henceforth be waged in data centres rather than living rooms. Yet artificial intelligence, that very same technological force which was meant to render everything frictionless, has instead devoured server capacity with such voracity that hardware manufacturers find themselves, rather ignominiously, returning to the business of selling physical components to actual human beings.

clips.text_en_b1: The anon is closer to a 1 plate OHP than he is to a 2 plate bench, 3 plate squat, or 4 plate deadlift. He thinks he will have a 1 plate OHP for reps in a month or two. Posted on /fit/ with picrel showing his physique.
clips.text_en_b2: My bench has completely fallen off a cliff lately, and I genuinely can't tell whether it's the cut wrecking my recovery or if my shoulders have simply packed it in. Right now a two-plate bench feels shaky at best, yet I keep telling people I'm chasing a four-plate deadlift, which sounds delusional written down. The fitcel crew insists I'm under-eating and need to pile in more rice, so I'll give that a shot, although finding time for the gym between licensing exam revision is becoming…
clips.text_en_c1: My bench press numbers have deteriorated rather precipitously of late, and I am genuinely uncertain whether the culprit is the aggressive caloric deficit I have been running or the simple fact that my shoulders have, despite my best efforts, failed to keep pace with my ambitions. At present, a two-plate bench feels alarmingly unstable, which renders talk of a four-plate deadlift somewhat aspirational; one suspects I am, in reality, considerably closer to a single-plate overhead press than to any of the milestones I had optimistically pencilled in.
clips.text_en_c2: There is a particular kind of quiet humiliation that attends a stalled bench press, the sort that prompts one to scrutinise every variable from caloric surplus to the integrity of one's rotator cuff. The situation is, by any reasonable measure, dire: a two-plate bench wobbles uncertainly overhead, while aspirations of a four-plate deadlift linger somewhere in the realm of fantasy, a goal so distant it might as well be inscribed on a distant planet. The overhead press, by contrast, hovers closer to a single plate, and progress on that lift appears, mercifully, a month or two within reach. Advice from well-meaning friends, typically involving additional rice and the cheerful injunction to eat more, is duly received, however impractical during examination season when neither gym nor kitchen admits of the requisite time.

clips.text_en_b1: Why do so many people seem to hate Demon Slayer, an anon asked on /a/. He is watching it for the first time and is on season 2. He says every criticism of the show applies equally, if not more, to other beloved anime, but those ones did not make billions of dollars.
clips.text_en_b2: Someone actually stuck up for Demon Slayer on /a/ and I'm still processing it. His argument was that most of the criticism boils down to jealousy over its success, since the same complaints could be lobbed at plenty of other beloved anime that simply didn't rake in billions. I powered through Season 2 recently and thought it was genuinely solid, even if the animation style isn't everyone's cup of tea.
clips.text_en_c1: An anonymous poster on /a/ has mounted what is, by the standards of that notoriously acerbic board, a remarkably measured defence of Demon Slayer, observing that the criticism levelled at the series appears to stem largely from its commercial ubiquity rather than any genuine artistic deficiency. He notes, with some justification, that the very same complaints could be transposed onto countless other beloved anime titles, yet those programmes escape scrutiny precisely because they did not generate billions in revenue.
clips.text_en_c2: There exists a rather curious phenomenon within anime discourse whereby works achieving genuine commercial success attract disproportionate criticism, a tendency the more cynical fans suggest owes less to aesthetic merit than to simple resentment of the mainstream. An anonymous contributor to /a/, currently working his way through Demon Slayer for the first time and now well into the second season, articulated the grievance with admirable clarity: virtually every criticism levelled at the series, he argued, could be applied with equal or greater force to other beloved titles, the only meaningful distinction being that those titles had not generated the sort of revenue that provokes resentment in the first place.
